Dear Reviewers and AC,

We sincerely thank you for your careful reviews and constructive feedback, which have greatly helped us improve our work. Below is a summary of our rebuttal:

**Recognition of Key Strengths**

We are pleased that the following strengths of our work were acknowledged:

- GaussianWorld Benchmark – a significant and timely benchmark for 3D Gaussian Splatting scene understanding. (Reviewer ymTm, w2HY, Vy2Q, U34u)

- Strong empirical evidence and insights on Language Gaussian Splatting (LGS) methods. (Reviewer ymTm, w2HY)

- Large-scale, high-quality dataset GaussianWorld-49K. (Reviewer w2HY, U34u)

- Clear, well-structured presentation. (Reviewer ymTm, Vy2Q)


**Addressed Concerns During Rebuttal**


- **Reviewer ymTm** – Added evaluation on background classes and 2D metrics; analyzed limitations of 2D-only and 3D-only metrics. Introduced a task-level evaluation on 3D object localization to diversify benchmark tasks. Clarified the benchmark’s adaptability for future LGS methods, addressed concerns about noisy 3D annotations, and detailed the label-voting setting.

- **Reviewer w2HY** – Clarified our motivation for standardizing benchmarking protocols and providing large-scale 3DGS datasets. Detailed our 3D evaluation metrics and explained the limited availability of generalizable methods.

- **Reviewer Vy2Q** – Provided real-world downstream use cases. Extended outdoor experiments to complex environments (KITTI-360) with 37 additional semantic classes. Analyzed the granularity of per-Gaussian language features.

- **Reviewer U34u** – Clarified the benchmark’s ability to handle different 3DGS reconstructions, presented ablations on CLIP features, and restated our motivation for using 3DGS representations.


We are encouraged by the positive feedback from Reviewer ymTm and Reviewer w2HY, who noted that most of their concerns were addressed, and we thank Reviewer Vy2Q for prompting a more systematic outdoor evaluation.

We hope these clarifications will help the committee fairly assess our contributions. All additional results and analyses will be included in the camera-ready version to further strengthen the paper. Once again, we sincerely thank you for your time and constructive input.

comment.value: We thank the reviewer for recognizing the value of the KITTI-360 evaluation and agree that SceneSplat's performance drop highlights limitation in the generalization ability of data-driven methods. As a feed-forward method trained exclusively on indoor data, its ability to distinguish the 4 broad outdoor classes in HoliCity (building, road, terrain, tree) was itself surprising to us. However, as semantic complexity increases in outdoor scenes (from 4 to 37 classes in KITTI-360), it cannot compete with per-scene processing methods that leverage pretrained outdoor-aware encoders like LSeg, as most classes like 'traffic signs' and 'traffic lights' never appear in the training data. To better understand complex outdoor scenes for data-driven methods, more diverse training data and domain-adaptive approaches are needed, which are important future work. Importantly, these results on outdoor scenes with varying semantic complexity help make our benchmark more comprehensive for evaluating Language Gaussian Splatting methods across realistic scenarios.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback. In the following, we address the main weaknesses that were raised.

**Inability to benchmark different 3DGS reconstructions.**

Our benchmarking protocols do not require having the same 3DGS reconstruction for all the reported evaluations. We realize that the 3D metric evaluation setup, described in L187–204 of the main paper and further detailed in Section B.1 of the supplementary material, is not fully clear. We plan to enhance the description of the evaluation protocol with the clarifications in the following. During the zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation, we evaluate using the 3D semantic labels at point clouds locations from the original data sources.

- From the language 3DGS field obtained from the method, each Gaussian primitive first receives a predicted semantic label based on the cosine similarity between its language feature and text query embeddings (Equation 1, lines 190-192).
- Then for each ground truth evaluation location in 3D, we find its K=25 nearest Gaussian neighbors and assign the majority-voted label from these neighbors as the semantic prediction for that location.

This K-NN voting protocol effectively transfers predictions from the 3DGS coordinates to the ground truth evaluation 3D points. Therefore, any 3DGS reconstruction configuration can be evaluated using the proposed benchmarking protocols. Furthermore, we have conducted the reported experiments on the same 3DGS reconstruction configurations since we already prepared 3DGS reconstructions of various scenes as part of our GaussianWorld-49k dataset. This also aligns well with the fact that most methods producing vision-language features on top of 3DGS are orthogonal to any reconstruction configuration. However, as explained above, one can also evaluate features computed on top of different 3DGS reconstructions with our benchmarking protocol. Therefore, methods that jointly reconstruct the scene and assign features can still be evaluated with our benchmark. Furthermore, the newly introduced 2D metric (under reviewer ymTm) is also compatible with any 3DGS reconstruction configuration.

**Restriction to CLIP features.**

We agree that the representation space should not be restricted to CLIP alone. That is why we have also conducted various experiments with the increasingly popular SigLIP2 representation space and compared the results to CLIP in L166-172 of the supplementary material, as well as Table F. Furthermore, the new discussion on the KITTI-360 outdoor evaluation under reviewer Vy2Q shows that LSeg features (used by Feature-3DGS and Gradient-Weighted 3DGS) stand out when it comes to outdoor environments. All these different findings illustrate the potential for improving LGS with better vision-language representation spaces, and we conclude that having better representation spaces is complementary to the development of LGS.

**Extending to advanced tasks**

We agree that scene understanding is a mature problem when it comes to 2D images. However, when it comes to open-vocabulary understanding of 3D scenes, we believe that the solutions are not yet mature. Tables 3–4 of the main paper clearly show that there is still a significant performance gap to fill in the best-performing Language Gaussian Splatting methods. Therefore, we focused on establishing a benchmark to systematically evaluate the progress of these methods. While we find the task of advanced 3D scene reasoning highly valuable and interesting, we view LGS as a complementary and foundational step. VLMs typically rely on extracted visual features when performing reasoning tasks. For instance, [1] builds a 3DGS reasoning VLM using one of the methods we benchmarked as its feature backbone, while [2] performs visual question answering using LGS features. In this work, we therefore concentrate on evaluating the capabilities and limitations of current approaches in open-vocabulary 3DGS understanding, which we see as a prerequisite for more advanced 3D reasoning. We also plan to explore and evaluate advanced reasoning tasks in our future work.

**Choice of 3DGS representation**

We believe that the rising trends of data-driven 3D reconstruction methods with pointmaps representations [3, 4] are very interesting and valuable. However, their main purpose is sensing and understanding the geometry. On the other hand, 3DGS still remain the best representation when it comes to immersive experiences and scene interactions, because of its unique ability to jointly encode appearance and geometry. Moreover, we see these two lines of work as complimentary to each other. We therefore chose to focus this work entirely on the 3DGS representation. Nevertheless, we are highly interested in exploring and evaluating the emerging pointmap-based representations in our future work, as we consider them a valuable and complementary line of research.

**Writing**

Thanks for pointing this out. We will work on improving the writing. Are there any specific sections or parts you think we should focus on more?

**References**

[1] A. M. Halacheva, J. N. Zaech, X. Wang, D. P. Paudel, and L. Van Gool, "GaussianVLM: Scene-centric 3D Vision-Language Models using Language-aligned Gaussian Splats for Embodied Reasoning and Beyond," *arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.00886*, Jul. 2025.

[2] A. Thai, S. Peng, K. Genova, L. Guibas, and T. Funkhouser, "Splattalk: 3d vqa with gaussian splatting," *arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.06271*, Mar. 2025.

[3] S. Wang, V. Leroy, Y. Cabon, B. Chidlovskii, and J. Revaud, “DUSt3R: Geometric 3D Vision Made Easy,” in Proc. IEEE/CVF Conf. Comput. Vis. Pattern Recognit. (CVPR), Jun. 2024.

[4] J. Wang, M. Chen, N. Karaev, A. Vedaldi, C. Rupprecht, and D. Novotny, “VGGT: Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer,” in Proc. Comput. Vis. Pattern Recognit. Conf. (CVPR), Jun. 2025.

We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback. We are delighted to hear that our paper is well-structured, with details clearly presented, and that it reads well. We are especially excited to hear that our proposed benchmark has strong potential for various applications and that experiment discussions are insightful. In the following, we address the weaknesses.

**Limited Evaluation Metrics**  

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to also consider background structures. In our initial submission, we followed the protocol of prior works like RegionPLC [1] and Mosaic3D [2], which report foreground-only metrics.  We have added the following evaluation: 1) mean IoU for only background classes: wall, floor, and ceiling, 2) mean IoU and accuracy across all classes, including background and foreground. Compared to foreground evaluation results in main paper Tables 3 and 4, the results show the same trend for background classes: generalizable method has better performance than per-scene optimization methods and per-scene optimization-free method. This indicates that background structures like walls, floors, and ceilings can be more effectively recognized through the data-driven approach.

Therefore, we have focused on the 3D metric, ensuring that methods are evaluated in the space where actions are made.

**Label Voting With K-Nearest Gaussian Neighbors**

In our GaussianWorld-49K dataset, there are no semantic segmentation labels attached to the Gaussians in the collected 3DGS scenes, which are optimized from the source 3D datasets respectively. During the zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation, we evaluate using the provided 3D semantic labels at point clouds locations. 

- From the language 3DGS field obtained from the method, each Gaussian primitive first receives a predicted semantic label based on the cosine similarity between its language feature and text query embeddings (Equation 1, lines 190-192).
- Then for each ground truth evaluation location, we find its K=25 nearest Gaussian neighbors and assign the majority-voted label from these neighbors as the semantic prediction for that location.

As the Gaussians are initialized from the point clouds locations (line 147-149), they densely distributes around them. This K-NN voting protocol effectively transfers predictions from the Gaussian coordinates to the ground truth evaluation points.

We acknowledge the reviewer's concerns about noisy 3D annotations and evaluation complexities.

- On noisy annotations, we agree that the 3D label quality varies among the source datasets. Moreover, our GaussianWorld benchmark evaluates on 1060 scenes in total, 50 times more scenes used than the baseline Language Gaussian Splatting methods, ensuring statistical significance despite local label noise.
- On inconsistencies across different 3D representations, could you help clarify what specific aspect you're referring to? If you mean label differences between 3DGS coordinates and point cloud annotations, our evaluation uses only the provided 3D semantic labels at point clouds locations, and the K-NN voting protocol specifically addresses that. If you're referring to other inconsistencies, we would appreciate clarification to better address the concern.

We believe our large-scale evaluation provides robust assessment despite the challenges for 3D data.

We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback. We are delighted that the reviewer recognizes our benchmark as unique and comprehensive. We are also happy to hear positive remarks about our ablations and scaling effects, as well as the clarity and structure of our paper. In the following, we address the main weaknesses that were raised.

**Real-world downstream use-cases**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the lack of description on real-world use cases. In the following, we will discuss several practical downstream use cases which directly benefit from Language Gaussian Splatting as the system backbone. Firstly, one important downstream task, as also pointed out by reviewer U34u, is advanced 3D scene reasoning with language. This task alone covers many interesting use cases like: scene discovery, immersive scene interactions, embodied long-horizon planning, navigation, etc. The task of advanced 3D scene reasoning is typically solved with spatial VLMs, which rely on having good quality features as input when performing reasoning tasks. For example, [1] builds a 3DGS reasoning VLM using one of the methods we benchmarked as its feature backbone, while [2] performs visual question answering using LGS features. Furthermore, LGS can be used as the system backbone for several other interesting use cases like: robotic grasping, 3D scene editing, localization, etc. Therefore, developing better LGS backbones directly contributes to the development of the above mentioned practical use cases.

**Limited classes in HoliCity benchmark**

We agree with the reviewer that evaluating on 4 classes of the HoliCity dataset limits the conclusions that can be drawn about the methods' performance in complex outdoor environments. Also, complex outdoor data sources are very scarce, especially ones suitable for evaluating LGS with a substantial number of scenes and semantic classes. Therefore, we extend our benchmark with evaluations on the KITTI-360 dataset [3].

In the KITTI-360 experiments, we observe that most methods are unable to effectively process large-scale scenes containing over 10 million Gaussians. Therefore, we divide each KITTI scene into 50 m × 50 m chunks. Under this setting, Feature-3DGS and Gradient-Weighted 3DGS achieve significantly better results compared to other methods. This performance gap likely stems from differences in 2D feature encoding: both well-performing methods employ LSeg (Language-driven Semantic Segmentation [4]), which is specifically pretrained on large-scale outdoor data and excels in outdoor scenes. In contrast, the underperforming methods rely on SAM-tiles-based features, which appear less effective in this setting. This trend is also observed in the Holicity experiments. Additionally, Feature-3DGS performs worse than Gradient-Weighted 3DGS, possibly due to its use of low-dimensional feature compression, which may lose discriminative detail compared to gradient-weighted aggregation. Furthermore, even though Feature-3DGS and Gradient-Weighted 3DGS performance stands out in complex outdoor settings, they do not stand out in indoor scenes because LSeg's patch-wise ViT encoding struggles to preserve fine object boundaries and small objects. While the data-driven method SceneSplat was trained exclusively on indoor data, our evaluation on KITTI demonstrates its ability to generalize to outdoor scenes, although extending its training data is vital to improve the outdoor performance.

**Granularity of per-Gaussian language features**

We analyze the correlation between per-Gaussian vision-language features and a variety of text queries across various environments through zero-shot semantic segmentation and scene query experiments, as reported quantitatively in main paper Tables 3–4. and illustrated qualitatively in main paper Figure 3. and 4.  In Figure 4. the query prompt *"These are fruits"* requires selecting very small and granular objects in 3D. Also, some other methods point to incorrect instances and unrelated regions such as catering bottles, regular bottles, or even the kitchen door, namely: OpenGaussian, Feature3DGS, and Gradient-Weighted 3DGS. Furthermore, more qualitative illustrations can be found in Figures C,D,E, and F of the supplementary material. We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback! 

We are pleased that our benchmark is recognized as both important and timely, and that our dataset is considered a valuable contribution to the 3D scene understanding community. We also appreciate the positive remarks regarding our taxonomy of core methods and our identification of key limitations in previous evaluation practices. Importantly, we share the belief that the proposed benchmark and dataset will encourage the development and training of foundation models. In the following, we address the weaknesses that were raised.


**Lack of novel models or algorithms**

We agree on the lack of novel methods and algorithms in our work. However, this work focuses on two key issues we identified in the ongoing development of the research field in Language Gaussian Splatting: 1) the lack of standardized benchmarking protocols for comprehensively evaluating newly developed methods; and 2) the absence of large-scale 3DGS datasets featuring complex scenes, which are essential for advancing the recent paradigm of generalizable 3D solutions. Moreover, advancing these two fronts requires substantial effort and resources. For this reason, we specifically chose to submit our work to the Datasets and Benchmarks track, as the expectations of this track align closely with our focus on establishing evaluation protocols and curating data resources, rather than on proposing new algorithms or models.


**Additional generalizable methods**

We agree that there is a bias on our conclusions about generalizable 3DGS scene understanding methods, since we evaluated only one method (SceneSplat). However, as far as we are aware, this is the only publicly available generalizable method when it comes to Language Gaussian Splatting. Furthermore, we hope that our encouraging findings inspire further development in this direction, which we plan to actively monitor and evaluate. If the reviewer has specific methods in mind, we would be happy to include them to draw more robust conclusions.


**Lack of 3D evaluation metrics discussion**

We thank the reviewer for highlighting the lack of clarity regarding our 3D evaluation setup and insufficient justification for the 3D evaluation metrics employed.

The evaluation setup is described in L187–204 of the main paper and further detailed in Section B.1 of the supplementary material. We plan to enhance the clarity of our description, including more details on K-nearest Gaussian neighbors voting. During the zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation, we evaluate using the provided 3D semantic labels at point clouds locations. 

- From the language 3DGS field obtained from the method, each Gaussian primitive first receives a predicted semantic label based on the cosine similarity between its language feature and text query embeddings (Equation 1, lines 190-192).
- Then for each ground truth evaluation location, we find its K=25 nearest Gaussian neighbors and assign the majority-voted label from these neighbors as the semantic prediction for that location.

As the Gaussians are initialized from the point clouds locations (line 147-149), they densely distributes around them. This K-NN voting protocol effectively transfers predictions from the Gaussian coordinates to the ground truth evaluation points.


In our 3D semantic evaluation, we use two metrics, mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) and mean Accuracy (mAcc). IoU is particularly suitable for 3D segmentation as it penalizes both false positives and false negatives, providing a balanced assessment. Its advantage lies in being robust to class imbalance during per-class averaging, ensuring that less common object categories receive equal weight as common ones. However, IoU can be sensitive to boundary area segmentation, which can be overly strict, especially to small objects as small misalignments can drastically reduce its IoU. Accuracy on the other hand is simpler, and focuses on true positive rates, but it doesn’t account for class imbalances. The two metrics are complementary, with mIoU generally considered the primary metric.


Finally, to make our benchmark fully reproducible, we publicly release the evaluation code for all the methods reported in the benchmark and our collected 3DGS dataset including the part that is used for evaluation.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper is well-structured and easy to follow. The dataset details are clearly presented through informative tables and figures.

2. The proposed benchmark, specifically tailored for generalizable 3D scene understanding, has strong potential for applications in various domains.

3. The experimental section provides insightful discussions of existing language-guided Gaussian Splatting methods.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Major weaknesses:

1. Limited Evaluation Metrics: The paper reports only two foreground-only 3D metrics, which may overestimate model performance and overlook background structures critical for downstream tasks like robotics and AR.

2. Missing 2D and Full-Scene Evaluation: Although the benchmark targets 3D scene understanding with vision-language grounding, it omits 2D evaluation and reports only foreground-only 3D metrics. In my opinion, a comprehensive benchmark should include both 2D and full-scene 3D evaluations to support real-world use cases and ensure fair comparison with prior work.

3. Unaddressed Challenges in 3D Evaluation: The paper advocates for 3D-based evaluation but does not justify the exclusion of widely used 2D metrics. This raises doubts about whether future methods will adopt the proposed protocol over existing practices. It also overlooks key issues in 3D evaluation, such as noisy annotations (e.g., in ScanNet, Matterport3D) and inconsistencies across different 3D representations.

4. Lack of Task-Level Evaluation: Existing language-guided Gaussian Splatting methods cover a variety of task settings, such as open-vocabulary segmentation, 3D object localization, and 3D object selection tasks. However, the proposed benchmark focuses solely on semantic segmentation and does not evaluate or support other task types, limiting its utility as a comprehensive benchmark.

1. For clarity, please include appropriate citations for all referenced methods and datasets at relevant points in the text (e.g., Table 2, Section 3.1).

summary.value:
This paper introduces GaussianWorld, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating vision-language understanding in 3D scenes represented via 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). The authors categorize existing approaches into three groups: (1) per-scene optimization-based, (2) per-scene optimization-free, and (3) generalizable methods. They highlight major limitations in current evaluation protocols, including the lack of standardized benchmarks, over-reliance on 2D projections, and scene-specific results.
To address these issues, the paper proposes:
•	A benchmark comprising 1,060 scenes and 325 semantic classes, covering both indoor and outdoor environments
•	A direct 3D-space evaluation protocol for segmentation and scene understanding tasks
•	A new dataset called GaussianWorld-49K, diverse scenes with 3DGS representations
•	Evaluation showing the superiority of generalizable models, especially cross-scene generalization
This work aims to lay the foundation for systematic and reproducible evaluation in 3D vision-language research, and to encourage the development of foundation models for 3DGS.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.	Timely and important benchmark contribution
The paper introduces GaussianWorld, a large-scale and diverse benchmark that enables standardized and realistic evaluation of 3D vision-language methods directly in 3D space.
2.	Clear problem framing and taxonomy
It provides a helpful categorization of existing methods (optimization-based, optimization-free, generalizable) and clearly identifies key limitations in current evaluation practices.
3.	Strong support for generalizable approaches
The benchmark demonstrates the effectiveness of generalizable methods, offering empirical evidence for their scalability, fast inference, and better performance across diverse scenes.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
•	Limited method-level innovation
While the benchmark and dataset contributions are valuable and timely, the paper does not introduce new models or algorithmic components. As a result, the work’s technical novelty may appear limited for readers expecting methodological innovation alongside infrastructure development.

•	Benchmark scope may still be biased
While the benchmark is extensive and well-designed, the evaluation of generalizable approaches relies on only a single prior method. This makes it difficult to draw robust conclusions about the paradigm as a whole. Including additional generalizable baselines would strengthen the claim that this approach is generally superior.

•	Lack of detailed 3D evaluation metrics discussion
The paper emphasizes 3D evaluation, but does not deeply discuss or justify the specific 3D metrics used (e.g., for segmentation), which may limit reproducibility or understanding of the evaluation setup.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
This paper makes a meaningful contribution to the 3D vision-language community by introducing GaussianWorld, the first large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate language-grounded 3D scene understanding directly in 3D space. The authors provide a clear problem formulation, highlighting key limitations in current evaluation protocols (e.g., reliance on 2D projections and limited scene diversity), and offer a practical solution through systematic benchmarking.

The GaussianWorld-49K dataset will likely serve as a valuable resource for training and evaluating generalizable 3DGS models, potentially accelerating progress in the field. The benchmark helps reveal the superiority of generalizable methods in terms of efficiency and cross-scene performance, supporting a shift away from scene-specific pipelines. One suggestion for improvement is to further expand and evaluate generalizable methods, possibly through baseline ablations or new architectural variations. Overall, this work is well-positioned to influence future research in 3D scene understanding, especially in encouraging the use of foundation models and scalable training.

final_justification.value: The additional explanations regarding the limited availability of generalizable methods and detailed clarification of the 3D evaluation metrics and their implementation significantly strengthened the paper. The improved clarity, along with the commitment to reproducibility through public release of datasets and evaluation code, effectively addressed my primary worries.

summary.value: This paper introduces GaussianWorld, the largest dataset and benchmark for Language Gaussian Splatting (LGS). It includes 49,000 indoor and outdoor scenes with over 26 billion Gaussians, spanning 4 datasets, 1,060 scenes, and 325 semantic classes.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This is the first large-scale benchmark focused on language-grounded 3D Gaussian Splatting.
2. Strong ablation studies and scaling effects.
3. Paper is easy to follow and well-organized.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Although technically impressive, the paper doesn’t clearly describe real-world downstream use cases where LGS and 3DGS benchmarks can apply.
2. The paper itself notes that the HoliCity benchmark has only 4 semantic classes. This limits the conclusions we can draw about the methods' performance in complex outdoor environments.
3. While the authors describe aligning Gaussians to image embeddings from vision-language models, it remains unclear how robust or semantically meaningful these annotations are, particularly for object categories with subtle distinctions. It would be helpful if the authors could provide more quantitative or qualitative evidence of the accuracy of the per-Gaussian language embeddings, such as through human evaluation or correlation with labeled semantic classes.

summary.value: This study introduces a large-scale dataset designed to evaluate the quality of current language-guided Gaussian understanding methods. Specifically, the dataset comprises 49K scenes, each containing Gaussian point clouds reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), along with their corresponding semantic labels and CLIP embeddings. This benchmark can be utilized to assess the effectiveness of various methods in lifting 2D CLIP embeddings to 3D space, with the evaluation metric being open-vocabulary semantic segmentation accuracy. The primary contribution of this work lies in proposing a comprehensive language-guided Gaussian understanding dataset that enables thorough evaluation of 2D-to-3D feature lifting performance.

strengths_contributions.value: This paper proposes GaussianWorld, a novel dataset for quantitative evaluation of language-guided 3D Gaussian understanding. Specifically, the authors reconstruct 49K scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to obtain Gaussian point clouds, which are then annotated with category labels and 2D-to-3D mapped CLIP embeddings. The most comparable work is ShapeSplat, which also captures large-scale (indoor) Gaussian point cloud scenes, but focuses on generalizable reconstruction, whereas GaussianWorld targets open-vocabulary semantic scene understanding.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The inherent flexibility in 3DGS reconstruction presents a fundamental limitation for this benchmark: the reconstruction results are not unique. Since semantic annotations are only provided for one specific 3DGS reconstruction outcome, methods employing joint reconstruction and feature extraction cannot be properly evaluated when their reconstruction results diverge from the benchmark's predefined 3DGS annotations, making feature metric assessment impossible.
2. The exclusive reliance on CLIP features warrants further justification. While the benchmark aims to evaluate 2D-to-3D feature mapping accuracy through open-vocabulary segmentation, this objective doesn't inherently require restricting the representation space to CLIP features alone. 
3. The scope of evaluation appears somewhat limited given current research progress. Open-vocabulary scene understanding has become relatively mature, suggesting potential for extending the benchmark to more advanced tasks like 3D scene reasoning.
4. The choice of 3DGS representation may not fully align with emerging trends. With the rise of data-driven 3D reconstruction paradigms, alternative representations like pointmap-based scene modeling are gaining traction. Developing benchmarks around such feed-forward-compatible representations might offer greater efficiency and better reflect current methodological directions.
5. The writing of this paper requires improvement.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: The dataset is constructed using publicly available multi-view datasets, employing open-source 3DGS reconstruction algorithms and CLIP feature extraction methods, thereby ensuring compliance with all ethical research standards.

Dataset URL: https://huggingface.co/datasets/GaussianWorld/gaussian_world_49k
Code URL: https://github.com/unique1i/GaussianWorld_Benchmark
All the URLs are publicly accessible and the dataset and code can be downloaded.

final_justification.value: These responses partially address my concerns, and I am inclined to maintain my current score. I look forward to future work where the authors design reasoning tasks or benchmarks that jointly tackle reconstruction and understanding in Gaussian-based scenarios.

title.value: SceneSplat++: A Large Dataset and Comprehensive Benchmark for Language Gaussian Splatting

abstract.value: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) serves as a highly performant and efficient encoding of scene geometry, appearance, and semantics. Moreover, grounding language in 3D scenes has proven to be an effective strategy for 3D scene understanding. Current Language Gaussian Splatting line of work fall into three main groups: (i) per-scene optimization-based, (ii) per-scene optimization-free, and (iii) generalizable approach. However, most of them are evaluated only on rendered 2D views of a handful of scenes and viewpoints close to the training views, limiting ability and insight into holistic 3D understanding. To address this gap, we propose the first large-scale benchmark that systematically assesses these three groups of methods directly in 3D space, evaluating on 1060 scenes across three indoor datasets and one outdoor dataset. Benchmark results demonstrate a clear advantage of the generalizable paradigm, particularly in relaxing the scene-specific limitation, enabling fast feed-forward inference on novel scenes, and achieving superior segmentation performance. We further introduce SceneSplat-49K -- a carefully curated 3DGS dataset comprising of around 49K diverse indoor and outdoor scenes trained from multiple sources, with which we demonstrate generalizable approach could harness strong data priors. Our codes, benchmark, and datasets are available at https://scenesplatpp.gaussianworld.ai/.

venue.value: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track poster

TLDR.value: We introduce SceneSplat-49K, a large 3DGS dataset spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, and provide a comprehensive benchmark SceneSplat-Bench for Language Gaussian Splatting methods.
